title: Apollo alternative for sequences, deliverability and CRM
author: Cryptool
excerpt_html: Apollo sells you a contact database with a sequencer attached. Reach is the sequencer and CRM without the database, and it is free. That trade matters.
content_html:
Apollo is really two products sold as one: a very large contact database, and an outreach engine that uses it. Teams that leave usually leave because they were paying database prices for the sequencer, or because the data quality on their particular niche did not justify the bill. Reach is a free investor and partner outreach tool that covers the sequencer, the CRM and the deliverability side. It does not have a contact database, and that is the honest headline of this comparison rather than a footnote.

What Apollo does well

The database is the product and it is a good one. Hundreds of millions of contacts, filters that let you build a list in minutes, and enrichment that fills in the gaps on a list you already have. If your motion is "define an ICP, pull ten thousand matching contacts, and start sending", Apollo does that in one place and very few tools genuinely compete with it. Nothing below argues against that.

The trade you are actually making

Reach has no contact database. You bring your list, by CSV import or by building it yourself, and the Sourcer agent will propose target firms and personas from your ICP with a search query for each, but it leaves the contact fields blank for you to verify. It does that deliberately, because a fabricated email address is worse than an empty one.

So if the database is why you use Apollo, keep using Apollo. If you already have your list, or your targets are the kind of people a general B2B database covers badly, which is true of most crypto funds, angels and syndicates, then the database is the part of the bill you are least served by.

What Reach covers

Sequences. Up to sixteen steps mixing email, LinkedIn, calls, SMS and manual tasks, with up to five A/B versions per step and per-version sent, open and reply stats so the winning version is flagged rather than guessed at.

Conditions and wait-steps. Each step can run always, or only if there was no reply, or if the message was opened, or clicked. More usefully, a step can wait for the condition instead of skipping it: park the follow-up until they open, with a timeout you set, and on timeout either skip or send anyway. Most sequencers only skip.

Email verification, built in and unmetered. Every address goes through syntax, domain MX, and an SMTP recipient probe that asks the receiving server whether the mailbox exists, stopping the conversation before anything is sent. Catch-all domains are detected with a control probe and reported as unconfirmed rather than passed off as good. There is no external service, no API key and no per-verification credit, and a send to an address that has never been checked verifies it first rather than gambling.

Your own mailboxes, with warm-up. Connect as many sending inboxes as you like, in bulk by CSV, with rotation, per-mailbox daily limits, warm-up and a test send from every mailbox before go-live. Capacity is the sum of your daily limits rather than a plan tier.

Safeguards that prevent the embarrassing send. Empty-snippet detection refuses to send a message with an unfilled merge tag, snippets take fallbacks so a blank field reads cleanly, and duplicate detection, suppression lists and unsubscribe handling are standard.

Replies, tracked properly. IMAP polling matches inbound mail to the prospect, logs it in the conversation and marks the enrollment replied, so stop-on-reply works without you touching it.

A CRM underneath. Prospects, pipeline, conversations, tasks and notes, plus a warm intro mapper that shows who in your imported network sits at the same firm as a prospect.

Choosing between them

Use Apollo if buying contact data is the job to be done. Use Reach if you have the list and want the sending, verification, deliverability and follow-up to be free and under your control. A number of teams do both, sourcing in one and running the campaign in the other, which is a perfectly reasonable answer.

Common questions

Does Reach include a contact database like Apollo?

No. You import your own list. The Sourcer agent proposes firms and personas to target from your ICP, but leaves contact details blank rather than inventing them. If you need bought contact data, Apollo is the better tool.

Is Reach free?

Yes, it comes with your Cryptool account. You connect your own sending mailboxes, so your sending capacity is not a plan tier.

Does Reach verify email addresses, or do I need a separate service?

It verifies them itself, with no external service and no per-check credits. Syntax, MX and an SMTP recipient probe, with catch-all detection, running in the background on your whole list and again before any first send.

Can Reach send LinkedIn messages automatically?

No. LinkedIn steps exist in a sequence but they are manual, opening the profile for you to act. Automating LinkedIn puts the account at risk, so we have not built it that way. X, Telegram and Discord adapters exist as stubs and are not wired.

How accurate is open tracking?

Approximately, like everywhere else. Open tracking uses a pixel, and image blockers and Apple Mail Privacy Protection inflate the numbers. Reply rate is the figure to trust, and it comes from actual IMAP reply matching.

Where do I start?

Open Reach with your Cryptool account, import a list, and build a sequence.
